This article fits a Poisson model in which every group has its own intercept
and its own slope, recovers the covariance of those group effects from
simulated data, and ends with guidance on how many groups a covariance needs.
Along the way it extracts the per-group effects, checks the fit, predicts for a
known and a new group, compares against a random-intercept model, and runs the
crossed, nested and uncorrelated formula terms. Installation is covered in
[Get started](tulpa.html).

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
```

## The covariance is the quantity of interest

A random-intercept model, `y ~ x + (1 | g)`, has a single variance
component: how much the groups differ in their baseline. A random-slope
model, `y ~ x + (1 + x | g)`, has three: the intercept variance, the
slope variance, and the correlation between them. That correlation is
often the scientific question (do groups that start high also respond
more steeply?), so it is inferred with its own uncertainty.

`tulpa()` treats the whole random-effect covariance $\Sigma$ as the inferred
object. When a term carries slopes, the fit integrates over $\Sigma$ instead of
conditioning on a plug-in value.

## The model

Index the groups by $j = 1, \ldots, J$ and the observations within group $j$ by
$i = 1, \ldots, n_j$. Let $y_{ij}$ be the count of observation $i$ in group $j$
and $x_{ij}$ its covariate. The count is Poisson with mean $\mu_{ij}$, and its
log is linear in the covariate with a group-specific intercept and slope,

$$
\log \mu_{ij} = (\beta_0 + b_{0j}) + (\beta_1 + b_{1j})\, x_{ij},
$$

where $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are the population intercept and slope (the fixed
effects) and $b_j = (b_{0j}, b_{1j})^\top$ is the deviation of group $j$ from
them (its random effects). The deviations are independent across groups and
share one bivariate normal distribution,

$$
b_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma), \qquad
\Sigma =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1^2 & \rho\, \sigma_1 \sigma_2 \\
\rho\, \sigma_1 \sigma_2 & \sigma_2^2
\end{pmatrix},
$$

with $\sigma_1$ the standard deviation of the group intercepts, $\sigma_2$ that
of the group slopes, and $\rho$ their correlation. The formula term
`(1 + x | g)` declares this full $\Sigma$; `(1 + x || g)` fixes $\rho = 0$.

The fit needs coordinates in which every value is a valid covariance matrix.
Write $\Sigma = L L^\top$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal (the
Cholesky factor). The three numbers

$$
\theta = \left(\log L_{11},\ \log L_{22},\ L_{21}\right)
$$

range over all of $\mathbb{R}^3$, and each $\theta$ gives a positive-definite
$\Sigma$. These log-Cholesky coordinates are the space the engine integrates
over; a diagonal block uses $\theta = (\log \sigma_1, \log \sigma_2)$ instead.
For a term with $c$ coefficients a full block has $c(c+1)/2$ coordinates and a
diagonal block $c$.

The integration has two layers. At a fixed $\theta$, a Laplace approximation
integrates out $\beta$ and every $b_j$ and returns the marginal likelihood of
$\theta$. Over $\theta$, a central composite design (CCD) places nodes around
the mode of that marginal likelihood, rotated by its curvature, and weights
each node by marginal likelihood times hyperprior. The default hyperprior is a
penalized-complexity (PC) prior on each $\sigma_i$ and an LKJ prior on the
correlation, described under [Priors on the covariance](#priors-on-the-covariance).
A reported $\sigma_1$, $\sigma_2$ or $\rho$ is a weighted quantile over the
nodes, so a skewed posterior keeps its skew.

## Simulating data

The simulation has 60 groups of 12 observations, a population intercept of
0.2 and a population slope of 0.5 on the log scale. The group intercepts vary
with standard deviation 0.7 and the group slopes with 0.5, at correlation 0.4:
groups with a higher baseline tend to respond more steeply to `x`.

```{r sim}
G   <- 60L                 # groups
npg <- 12L                 # observations per group
N   <- G * npg
grp <- rep(seq_len(G), each = npg)
x   <- rnorm(N)

# True Sigma: sd 0.7 (intercept), 0.5 (slope), correlation 0.4.
Sigma <- matrix(c(0.7^2,            0.4 * 0.7 * 0.5,
                  0.4 * 0.7 * 0.5,  0.5^2), 2)
u <- t(t(chol(Sigma)) %*% matrix(rnorm(2 * G), 2))   # G x 2 group effects
eta <- 0.2 + 0.5 * x + u[grp, 1] + u[grp, 2] * x
y   <- rpois(N, exp(eta))
d   <- data.frame(y = y, x = x, g = factor(grp))
head(d, 3)
```

`u` holds the true group effects, one row per group: column 1 the intercept
deviation $b_{0j}$, column 2 the slope deviation $b_{1j}$. They are kept so
that the per-group estimates can be compared with them below.

## Fitting

A `(1 + x | g)` term with `mode = "laplace"` routes the fit to the
nested-Laplace integration over $\Sigma$ (`tulpa_re_cov_nested()`).

```{r fit}
fit <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d, family = "poisson",
             mode = "laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
fit
```

The printed header names the backend, `re_cov_nested`. `fixef()` returns the
population intercept and slope, and `summary()` adds their intervals.

```{r fixef}
fixef(fit)
summary(fit)$coefficients
```

`VarCorr()` reports the standard deviation of each random-effect coefficient;
its `cov` attribute holds the posterior mean of $\Sigma$, with the correlation
matrix attached.

```{r varcorr}
vc <- VarCorr(fit)
vc
attr(vc, "cov")$g
```

The full posterior summary of the covariance is the `hyperparameters` table of
`summary()`: the two standard deviations, the correlation, and the three
entries of $\Sigma$, each with a 95% interval.

```{r hyper}
summary(fit)$hyperparameters[, c("parameter", "median", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
```

The intervals contain the true $\sigma_1 = 0.7$, $\sigma_2 = 0.5$ and
$\rho = 0.4$. The correlation interval also contains zero: with 60 groups the
data cannot separate a correlation of 0.4 from none.

`ranef()` returns one row per group and coefficient. Terms named `g[j]` are the
intercept deviations and `g.x[j]` the slope deviations; `estimate`, `sd` and
the interval come from the node mixture (`source = "mixture"`), so they carry
both the within-node uncertainty and the uncertainty in $\Sigma$.

```{r ranef}
re <- as.data.frame(ranef(fit))
head(re, 4)
```

## Interpreting the per-group effects

Split the table into intercepts and slopes, line each up with its true value,
and count how many intervals contain the truth.

```{r ranef-split}
re_int <- re[grepl("^g\\[", re$term), ]
re_slp <- re[grepl("^g\\.x\\[", re$term), ]
c(intercept = mean(re_int$conf.low <= u[, 1] & u[, 1] <= re_int$conf.high),
  slope     = mean(re_slp$conf.low <= u[, 2] & u[, 2] <= re_slp$conf.high))
range(re_slp$conf.high - re_slp$conf.low)   # slope interval widths
```

The figure orders the groups by their estimated slope deviation and draws each
95% interval with the true value as an open circle.

```{r ranef-plot, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Estimated slope deviation for each of the 60 groups with its 95 percent interval, ordered by estimate, with the true simulated slope deviation drawn as an open circle on each interval"}
o <- order(re_slp$estimate)
plot(seq_len(G), re_slp$estimate[o], pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     ylim = range(re_slp$conf.low, re_slp$conf.high, u[, 2]),
     xlab = "group (ordered by estimate)", ylab = "slope deviation b1")
segments(seq_len(G), re_slp$conf.low[o], seq_len(G), re_slp$conf.high[o],
         col = "grey50")
points(seq_len(G), u[o, 2], pch = 1, col = "darkorange")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("estimate and 95% interval", "truth"),
       pch = c(19, 1), col = c("black", "darkorange"), bty = "n")
```

The slope intervals contain the true deviation for 59 of the 60 groups, and
the intercept intervals for 57. The slope interval widths range from
`r if (EVAL_FITS) round(min(re_slp$conf.high - re_slp$conf.low), 2) else "(computed when built)"`
to `r if (EVAL_FITS) round(max(re_slp$conf.high - re_slp$conf.low), 2) else "(computed when built)"`,
so a slope estimated for one group can be much less certain than the slope of
its neighbour in the ordering.

## Checking the fit

A predictive check simulates replicate data sets from the posterior and
compares them with the observed counts. On the nested fit, `posterior_predict()`
draws each replicate's fixed effects from one integration node and the group
effects jointly with them from that node's Gaussian, so every replicate carries
the group lines. `pp_check()` overlays the density of 50 replicate data sets on
the observed counts and returns a ggplot; the counts reach above 100 in a few
steep groups, so the plot is cut at 15 to show the bulk.

```{r ppcheck, fig.alt = "Densities of 50 posterior predictive replicate count data sets overlaid on the density of the observed counts, for counts from 0 to 15"}
pp_check(fit) + ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 15))
```

The observed density lies inside the band of replicates over the whole range.

`check_model()` gives the formal version: a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the
randomized PIT residuals against the uniform distribution (`ks_p`), and the
ratio of observed to replicated variance (`disp_ratio`, near 1 when the model
reproduces the spread of the data).

It also draws three panels: the PIT residuals against the uniform quantiles,
Pearson residuals against fitted values, and the observed variance against
its replicate distribution.

```{r checkmodel, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Three diagnostic panels: PIT residuals against uniform quantiles, Pearson residuals against fitted values, and the observed variance of the counts against its distribution over replicate data sets"}
cm <- check_model(fit)
unlist(cm)
```

`ks_p` is `r if (EVAL_FITS) round(cm$ks_p, 2) else "(computed when built)"`
and `disp_ratio` is `r if (EVAL_FITS) round(cm$disp_ratio, 2) else "(computed when built)"`:
the PIT residuals are consistent with uniformity and the replicates reproduce
the spread of the counts. The middle panel reads `fitted()`, which returns the
conditional mean with each group's own effect;
`fitted(fit, effects = "population")` holds the group effects at zero.

The exact Metropolis-within-Gibbs fit samples $\Sigma$ and the group effects
together and gives an independent read of the covariance. Ask for it with
`control$re_cov = "gibbs"`.

```{r fit-gibbs}
fit_gibbs <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d, family = "poisson",
                   mode = "laplace",
                   control = list(re_cov = "gibbs", n_iter = 2000L,
                                  warmup = 1000L, n_threads = 2))
summary(fit_gibbs)$hyperparameters[1:3, c("parameter", "median",
                                          "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
```

The sampler and the nested integration agree on all three covariance
parameters to within 0.02.

## Prediction

`predict()` conditions on the groups named in `newdata`. With `re_form = NA` it
returns the population-level prediction: fixed effects only, random effects at
zero.

```{r predict-pop}
nd  <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 41))
pop <- predict(fit, newdata = nd, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE, re_form = NA)
head(pop, 3)
```

A new group draws its own $b = (b_0, b_1)^\top$ from $\mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$.
At covariate $x$ its linear predictor adds $b_0 + b_1 x$, whose variance is
$z^\top \Sigma z$ with $z = (1, x)^\top$. A group label the fit did not see
gets that predictive interval: `predict()` reads it over joint draws of the
fixed effects and of $b$, with $\Sigma$ drawn from its posterior.

```{r predict-new}
new <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(nd, g = "new"), type = "link",
               se.fit = TRUE)
round(c(pop_width = pop$upper[21] - pop$lower[21],
        new_width = new$upper[21] - new$lower[21]), 2)
```

At $x = 0$ the link-scale interval for a new group is about seven times wider
than the population interval, because it carries the spread of group
intercepts. A known group instead takes its own posterior effect: a label the
fit saw draws that group's intercept and slope jointly with the fixed effects.
The figure shows the population and new-group bands on the count scale, with
the fitted lines and bands of the two groups with the smallest and largest
estimated slope.

```{r predict-plot, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Expected count against x for the population with its 95 percent band, a wider 95 percent band for a new unobserved group, and the fitted lines with 95 percent bands of the two groups with the smallest and largest estimated slope"}
jj <- levels(d$g)[c(which.min(re_slp$estimate), which.max(re_slp$estimate))]
known <- lapply(jj, function(gj)
  predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(nd, g = gj), type = "link", se.fit = TRUE))
band <- function(p, col) polygon(c(nd$x, rev(nd$x)),
                                 exp(c(p$lower, rev(p$upper))),
                                 col = col, border = NA)
plot(nd$x, exp(pop$fit), type = "n", ylim = c(0, 8),
     xlab = "x", ylab = "expected count")
band(new, adjustcolor("grey60", 0.3))
band(pop, adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.4))
lines(nd$x, exp(pop$fit), lwd = 2)
for (k in seq_along(known)) {
  band(known[[k]], adjustcolor("darkorange", 0.2))
  lines(nd$x, exp(known[[k]]$fit), lty = k + 1, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
}
legend("topleft", c("population (95%)", "new group (95%)",
                    "flattest group", "steepest group"),
       fill = c(adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.4), adjustcolor("grey60", 0.3),
                NA, NA), border = NA, lty = c(NA, NA, 2, 3),
       col = c(NA, NA, "darkorange", "darkorange"),
       bg = adjustcolor("white", 0.85), box.col = "grey80")
```

## Comparing against a random-intercept model

Does the slope variance earn its place? Fit `(1 | g)` on the same data and
compare model evidence. Two settings matter. Under `mode = "laplace"` a plain
`(1 | g)` term conditions on a supplied `sigma_re`; `control$re_cov = "nested"`
integrates its scale like any other covariance block. And `logLik()` on a CCD
design declines to report an evidence, so both fits use the tensor-product
grid (`integration = "grid"`), on which the evidence is read under the
hyperprior.

```{r compare}
ctl <- list(integration = "grid", n_threads = 2)
fit_slp <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d, family = "poisson",
                 mode = "laplace", control = ctl)
fit_int <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "poisson",
                 mode = "laplace", control = c(ctl, list(re_cov = "nested")))
compare_models(intercept = fit_int, slopes = fit_slp, criterion = "loglik")
```

The log evidence of the random-slope model is higher by
`r if (EVAL_FITS) round(as.numeric(logLik(fit_slp)) - as.numeric(logLik(fit_int)), 1) else "(computed when built)"`
nats. The evidence integrates over $\Sigma$ under its prior, so it already
charges the slope model for its two extra covariance parameters.
`compare_models(criterion = "waic")` and `"loo"` also run on the nested door,
on replicates that carry the per-group effects.

## Formula syntax

Each term inside `( | )` becomes one covariance block, and every block is
integrated. The fits below run on the data above or on small variants of it.

| Term | Covariance block |
|---|---|
| `(1 \| g)` | 1 x 1: intercept SD |
| `(1 + x \| g)` | 2 x 2 full: two SDs and a correlation |
| `(1 + x \|\| g)` | 2 x 2 diagonal: two SDs, correlation fixed at 0 |
| `(1 \| g) + (1 \| h)` | two 1 x 1 blocks, crossed factors |
| `(1 \| site/plot)` | two 1 x 1 blocks, `site` and `site:plot` |

### Uncorrelated slopes

`||` drops the correlation, leaving two log-SD coordinates.

```{r diag}
fit_diag <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x || g), data = d, family = "poisson",
                  mode = "laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
VarCorr(fit_diag)
```

The two standard deviations are close to those of the correlated fit. With
the true $\rho = 0.4$ and an interval for $\rho$ that contains zero, the
diagonal block loses little here.

### Crossed factors

Crossed factors are groupings that do not nest, such as observer and site: each
observer visits many sites and each site has many observers. The simulation
adds a second factor `h` with 15 levels assigned at random, with intercept SD
0.5.

```{r crossed}
set.seed(3)
h  <- factor(sample(1:15, N, replace = TRUE))
yc <- rpois(N, exp(0.2 + 0.5 * x + u[grp, 1] + rnorm(15, 0, 0.5)[h]))
dc <- data.frame(y = yc, x = x, g = factor(grp), h = h)
fit_crossed <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g) + (1 | h), data = dc,
                     family = "poisson", mode = "laplace",
                     control = list(re_cov = "nested", n_threads = 2))
VarCorr(fit_crossed)
```

The true intercept SDs are 0.7 for `g` (the same `u[, 1]` as above) and 0.5
for `h`.

### Nested factors

Nested factors are groupings where each level of the inner one sits inside a
single level of the outer one: 5 plots inside each of 12 sites here, with SD
0.6 between sites and 0.3 between plots within a site. `(1 | site/plot)`
expands to `(1 | site) + (1 | site:plot)`, so plot labels can repeat across
sites.

```{r nested}
site <- factor(rep(1:12, each = 60))
plot_id <- factor(rep(1:5, each = 12, times = 12))
sp   <- interaction(site, plot_id)
yn   <- rpois(N, exp(0.2 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(12, 0, 0.6)[site] +
                       rnorm(60, 0, 0.3)[sp]))
dn   <- data.frame(y = yn, x = x, site = site, plot = plot_id)
fit_nested <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | site/plot), data = dn,
                    family = "poisson", mode = "laplace",
                    control = list(re_cov = "nested", n_threads = 2))
VarCorr(fit_nested)
```

## Priors on the covariance

The default hyperprior of a full block is built by `re_cov_pc_lkj_prior()`. Each
standard deviation gets a PC prior, an exponential distribution calibrated by
`prior_sigma = c(U, alpha)` so that $P(\sigma_i > U) = \alpha$; the default is
$P(\sigma_i > 3) = 0.01$. The correlation matrix gets an LKJ prior with shape
`eta`, density proportional to $\det(R)^{\eta - 1}$, which for a 2 x 2 block is
$(1 - \rho^2)^{\eta - 1}$. The default `eta = 2` favours weak correlations
mildly; `eta = 1` is uniform on $\rho$. The function returns the log density in
the block's log-Cholesky coordinates, Jacobian included, so it can be read at
the true $\Sigma$ directly.

```{r prior-eval}
L <- t(chol(Sigma))
theta_true <- c(log(L[1, 1]), log(L[2, 2]), L[2, 1])
lp2 <- re_cov_pc_lkj_prior(2)
lp4 <- re_cov_pc_lkj_prior(2, eta = 4)
c(eta2 = lp2(theta_true), eta4 = lp4(theta_true))
```

At the front door, the same two settings are passed as
`re_prior = list(prior_sigma =, eta =)`. Three priors on the same data show
how much they move the posterior: the default, a tighter scale prior
$P(\sigma_i > 1) = 0.01$ with `eta = 4`, and a uniform correlation prior.

```{r prior-sens}
priors <- list(default = NULL,
               tight   = list(prior_sigma = c(1, 0.01), eta = 4),
               uniform = list(eta = 1))
sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(priors), function(p) {
  f <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d, family = "poisson",
             mode = "laplace", re_prior = priors[[p]],
             control = list(n_threads = 2))
  h <- summary(f)$hyperparameters[1:3, ]
  data.frame(prior = p, parameter = h$parameter, median = round(h$median, 3),
             ci_lo = round(h$ci_lo, 3), ci_hi = round(h$ci_hi, 3))
}))
sens
```

With 60 groups the medians move by a few hundredths across the three priors,
and the tighter prior shifts all three parameters slightly toward zero. The
Gibbs backend uses a conjugate inverse-Wishart prior instead, set through
`re_prior = list(prior_df =, prior_scale =)`.

## Small binary groups: when the exact sampler matters

The Laplace approximation inside each node treats every group's likelihood as
Gaussian in $b_j$. For binary responses in small groups that likelihood is far
from Gaussian, and the approximation pulls the variance components low. The
Gibbs sampler draws $\Sigma$ from its exact conditional distribution, an
inverse-Wishart, given the sampled $b_j$, and does not have that bias.

The simulation below has 50 groups of 6 binary observations, true $\sigma_1 =
1$, $\sigma_2 = 0.7$ and $\rho = 0$. Each of 20 replicate data sets is fitted
with both backends. The table averages the posterior medians of the two
standard deviations and counts the fits whose slope SD collapsed (posterior
median below 0.05).

```{r binary-sim}
sim_bin <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  gg <- rep(1:50, each = 6)
  xx <- rnorm(300)
  b0 <- rnorm(50, 0, 1)
  b1 <- rnorm(50, 0, 0.7)
  yy <- rbinom(300, 1, plogis(-0.3 + 0.8 * xx + b0[gg] + b1[gg] * xx))
  data.frame(y = yy, x = xx, g = factor(gg))
}
```

```{r binary-compare, warning = FALSE}
med3 <- function(f) summary(f)$hyperparameters$median[1:3]
reps <- sapply(1:20, function(s) {
  db <- sim_bin(s)
  fn <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = db, family = "binomial",
              mode = "laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
  fg <- suppressWarnings(tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = db,
              family = "binomial", mode = "laplace",
              control = list(re_cov = "gibbs", n_iter = 2000L,
                             warmup = 1000L, n_threads = 2)))
  c(med3(fn), med3(fg))
})
data.frame(truth     = c(1, 0.7),
           nested    = round(rowMeans(reps[1:2, ]), 3),
           gibbs     = round(rowMeans(reps[4:5, ]), 3),
           row.names = c("sigma_1", "sigma_2"))
c(nested = sum(reps[2, ] < 0.05), gibbs = sum(reps[5, ] < 0.05))
```

The loop hides its warnings to keep the output readable. The Gibbs fits warn
about chain length, and the nested fits of replicates whose slope SD collapses
repeat a warning that the marginal fixed-effect precision could not be formed.
On a single analysis they are worth reading.
Averaged
over the replicates, the nested Laplace estimates both standard deviations
below their true values, the slope SD most (0.45 against 0.7), and in 5 of
the 20 replicates it places the slope SD at zero. The Gibbs averages are
within 0.1 of the truth, and none of its fits collapses.

### Adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature

A deterministic alternative keeps the nested integration over $\Sigma$ and
replaces the per-group Laplace step by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature with
`n_quad` points per dimension (`control$re_cov = "aghq"`). `n_quad = 1` is the
Laplace step; higher orders integrate each group's non-Gaussian likelihood more
accurately. It costs far more than the Laplace step: the call below, on one of
the binary data sets, takes about 50 seconds where the Laplace fit takes about
20.

```{r aghq}
db1 <- sim_bin(1)
fit_aghq <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = db1, family = "binomial",
                  mode = "laplace",
                  control = list(re_cov = "aghq", n_quad = 3L, n_threads = 2))
summary(fit_aghq)$hyperparameters[1:3, c("parameter", "median",
                                         "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
round(reps[, 1], 3)   # nested Laplace, then Gibbs, on the same data set
```

`reps[, 1]` holds the nested and Gibbs medians of $\sigma_1$, $\sigma_2$ and
$\rho$ for the same data set. Quadrature of order 3 raises both standard
deviations above the Laplace values: $\sigma_1$ from 0.45 to 0.54, against
0.65 from the Gibbs sampler, and $\sigma_2$ from 0.80 to 0.91, against 0.99.

## How many groups a covariance needs

The interval for a correlation narrows slowly with the number of groups,
because each group contributes one noisy pair $(b_{0j}, b_{1j})$. The sweep
below refits the Poisson model of the first sections at 10, 20, 40 and 80
groups, three data sets each, and reports the median width of the 95% interval
for $\sigma_2$ and $\rho$. A fit whose slope SD collapses to zero has no
interval for $\rho$; the `collapsed` column counts those fits, and the width
of $\rho$ is the median over the others.

```{r groups-sweep}
sim_pois <- function(G, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  gg <- rep(seq_len(G), each = npg)
  xx <- rnorm(G * npg)
  uu <- t(t(chol(Sigma)) %*% matrix(rnorm(2 * G), 2))
  yy <- rpois(G * npg, exp(0.2 + 0.5 * xx + uu[gg, 1] + uu[gg, 2] * xx))
  data.frame(y = yy, x = xx, g = factor(gg))
}
sweep <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(10L, 20L, 40L, 80L), function(G) {
  w <- sapply(1:3, function(s) {
    h <- summary(tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = sim_pois(G, s),
                       family = "poisson", mode = "laplace",
                       control = list(n_threads = 2)))$hyperparameters
    k <- match(c("sigma_2", "rho_12"), h$parameter)
    c(h$median[k[1]], (h$ci_hi - h$ci_lo)[k])
  })
  data.frame(groups = G, collapsed = sum(w[1, ] < 0.05),
             width_sigma_2 = round(median(w[2, ]), 2),
             width_rho = round(median(w[3, ], na.rm = TRUE), 2))
}))
sweep
```

## Practical guidance

The numbers below come from the fits in this article: Poisson counts with 12
observations per group, and binary responses with 6.

| Situation | Measured here | Choice |
|---|---|---|
| 10 groups, full 2 x 2 block | $\rho$ interval width 1.20 of 2; 1 of 3 fits collapsed the slope SD | read $\rho$ as unidentified; drop the correlation or the slope |
| 20 to 40 groups | $\rho$ width 0.93 to 0.78 | $\rho$ gives its sign at best |
| 80 groups | $\rho$ width 0.49, $\sigma_2$ width 0.21 | the full block is informed |
| 6 binary observations per group | nested $\sigma_2$ 0.45 against 0.7; 5 of 20 fits collapsed | `control$re_cov = "gibbs"` |
| 12 Poisson observations per group | nested and Gibbs medians within 0.02 on every parameter | nested Laplace |

- A full block of $c$ coefficients has $c(c+1)/2$ covariance parameters,
  three for an intercept and one slope. The sweep above suggests budgeting
  several tens of groups before reading the correlation, and treating a fit
  with fewer than about 20 groups as informative about the standard
  deviations only.

- When the interval for $\rho$ covers zero, `(1 + x || g)` keeps both standard
  deviations with one parameter fewer. In the example its SDs differed by 0.02
  or less from those of the correlated fit.

- Compare a slope model against the random-intercept model with both fits on
  `integration = "grid"`, as in
  [Comparing against a random-intercept model](#comparing-against-a-random-intercept-model).
  The evidence already charges the slope model for its extra parameters.

- With 60 groups the three priors above moved the medians by 0.03 or less.
  With fewer groups the prior carries more of the posterior, so refit with a
  tighter `prior_sigma` and with `eta = 1` and compare.

- A random slope needs the covariate to vary within each group. If `x` takes
  one value per group, $b_{1j} x_j$ cannot be told apart from $b_{0j}$ and the
  slope variance is not identified; leave the slope out.
